hits.text:
Creatine didn't build muscle or burn fat in this study. It was water retention. 

Exercise wasn't randomized. Participants chose whether to train. 

DEXA scans count water as "lean mass". Creatine hydrated muscle cells. It didn't synthesize new contractile fibers.  

The drop in body fat percentage was due to the math of adding water weight.
hits.draft_en:

Fair enough. A tub of powder won't do the work for you.

Past 50, the muscle comes from lifting heavy things often, eating enough protein and sleeping. Get those three sorted first. Then worry about what's in the shaker.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
About one cup of whole blueberries per day is the dose that overlaps most consistently with the positive human evidence.

The clearest benefit is vascular. Blueberries improve endothelial function, the ability of arteries to relax and deliver more blood when tissues need it.

Studies also suggest selected memory benefits in older adults with cognitive vulnerability. Improvements in insulin sensitivity or post-meal glucose handling appear more likely when metabolism is already under strain. Findings for gut health and exercise recovery are promising but less consistent.

Randomized trials have not shown that blueberries prevent dementia, diabetes, heart attacks, or strokes. But one cup (roughly 150 to 180 grams) of fresh or frozen blueberries per day is a practical, evidence-based target with benefits extending well beyond a simple “antioxidant” effect.

I cover all of this and more in the latest episode of the podcast!

hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
Am I a madman or messiah? 

I’m not going to feign humility or pretend I’ve stumbled into this. For 30 years I’ve worked to create something of enduring value for the human race.

My primary education has come from reading biographies. You can read a book on World War II and learn how the Germans did this, and the Americans did that. Autobiographies, by contrast, preserve the high resolution nuance that broad histories discard, capturing the raw psychology and lived friction of the era.

Biographies speak to me because they represent the rare artifacts that survived the brutal compression of time. Every generation’s existence is compressed by around 90%. That means, 90% of people and things that seemed immortal during their time are erased from history in a single generation. It’s simply too much information for humans to carry forward. Three generations of compression means that 99.9% of human activity is forgotten, leaving only one in a thousand figures, ideas, or works to cross the threshold into cultural memory.

Humans solve this information overload by encoding entire epochs into a single person, event, work, institution or idea. These distilled archetypes become required information for the species to tell its own story.

Going deep into biographies in my 20s, I could see these patterns: an infinite depth of human experience continuously compressed into durable memetic code.

I felt inspired by this idea and by the people I was learning about. I specifically admired those, who in their time and place, were able to identify the central defining issue of their time. They didn’t do what others were doing. They didn’t by default pursue the status games of their era. They sought out what I call Zeros.  

Schopenhauer drew this distinction: 

> Talent hits a target no one else can hit. (First principle thinking)

> Genius hits a target no one else can see. (Zeroth principle thinking)

I wondered:
> what will be the Zero of my lifetime? 
> what is currently invisible yet will be the only thing history will see? 
> can I find it and build it? 

I’ve been pursuing this goal since I was 21 years old. Without having any real talent, struggling as a student, having a humble upbringing, and no world connections, I set a goal of becoming independently wealthy by age 30. Then, with money, I reasoned, I’d set my focus on becoming a Zero detective and a Zero builder. 

At age 34, I sold Braintree Venmo in 2013 for $800M, making $300M of that. 

It was now time to become a zero detective.

The problem was that I was cooked as a human. The fourteen years of entrepreneurship, young children, existentially wrestling with my spirituality, and a challenging relationship left me chronically depressed, overweight, inflamed, recently divorced, and without meaning. First, I’d have to rebuild myself to stabilize. Health became my stabilization. I didn't know it then, but the thing I did to survive would turn out to be the thing I was looking for.

I obsessively got to work searching for a Zero. I became a voracious reader and thought about it constantly. I hosted a dozen dinners across the U.S., posing the question to attendees, “Imagine we’re in 2050 and life is extraordinary, what did we focus on in 2016 to make that happen?” I’d carefully write down everyone’s ideas and then after the dinner series, I put them down on a piece of paper, drew a box around them, and then told myself I couldn’t do anything inside the box.

Still, I couldn’t see, feel or hear a Zero. 

I then did a thought experiment that did it for me. I imagined being present in the year 2500 and sat there listening to them converse. They were talking about homo sapiens who lived in the early 21st century and they expressed their gratitude saying “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who did __________ and __________.”

What do they say? 

What would survive 500 years of compression? 

I thought about this question for years.

Then one day the answer came to me, they say: “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who gave birth to superintelligence and figured out they’d no longer die.” 

Our century compressed into two artifacts.

Superintelligence will be built whether or not I’m around. The other artifact was wide open. It would be a turning point in intelligent life. Transitioning from everyone inevitably dies (YOLO) to we are the first generation who won’t die. Changing everything about how we think about life and death, other people, the planet and our precious, fragile existence. 

Don’t Die is the Zero.

A tectonic shift in human values from being willing to kill themselves and others for power, wealth and status, to valuing existence itself above all other rewards. 

Wanting to live is the most ordinary desire a human has, which makes it a strange thing to call invisible. Very few actually want to die, at least today. Yet almost nobody organizes their life around not dying because for all of history it was unachievable. It makes more rational sense to pursue immediate hedonic, status and power objectives and to lean on the elaborate philosophies the species has made to make peace with death.

The era of Don’t Die will commence in 2030. New age reversal therapies will emerge and AI automation will run our lives, removing the biggest blockers of health: discipline and effort. Death acceptance will vanish as fast as body positivity did with GLP-1s.

(The irony here is that if Don’t Die is a Zero, and it comes to pass, then the 90% compression that has been the rule may stop being the rule.)

Kate and I are building for this. 

We do serious experimentation on health. 
We are performance artists.
We are memetic representations.
We are building a philosophy and ideology.
We are building the infrastructure for the species to turn its attention and power to Don’t Die.

If you’ve ever felt inspired, like me, by people of the past, who were willing to be hated, ridiculed, and dismissed in their pursuit of a Zero, the above should give you motivation. You will have to suffer through a prolonged period trying to find and build a Zero but the reward is being of service to the long arc of intelligent existence in this part of the galaxy.
hits.draft_skip_reason: repeat from 7 Oct; not drafted then (madman or messiah essay, off lane)

PBCC was the single most requested flavor of the protein bar, so we had to see if this issue was solvable. 

Contrary to the convenient narrative, I didn’t just want to make another protein bar flavor for $, I wanted to make something of the highest quality possible.

Turns out this issue was solvable. We found the best peanuts on the planet, with the lowest amount of linoleic acid. Peanuts are normally 15-20% LA, we found peanuts that were 2-3% LA. This extends shelf life and prevents rancidity (oxidation) massively.

We also tested our peanuts for mold toxins like aflatoxin and other contaminants like heavy metals. What other company does this? What other protein bar is this intentional about their ingredients?

Look, you want protein? Eat real food first. Eat steak, chicken, eggs, milk- whatever you want if you have time to prep it. But if you are on the go and want the convenience of a protein bar that is not garbage, we’ve made something incredible for you, and I am proud of it. There’s nothing better on the market, full stop.

You can find all of the lineage protein bar flavors (chocolate chip cookie dough, peanut butter chocolate chip, mixed berry, coconut macadamia, and chocolate brownie) at https://t.co/NK1uHBUMGm. < 200 cal, 20g grass fed whey protein and collagen, tallow, and honey. No artificial flavors, no natural flavors, no stevia, no fiber syrups- only real food, incredible taste.

I’m happy when people try to criticize these bars, it’s just more of an opportunity to show how good they really are and how hard we worked to make them the best.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Regular blueberry intake has been linked to slower cognitive aging.

Older women in the Nurses Health Study who ate at least half a cup of blueberries per week experienced slower cognitive decline than women who rarely ate them. The estimated difference was equivalent to being roughly 1.5 to 2.5 years younger cognitively.

Furthermore, people who consume blueberries at least occasionally have been shown to experience a one-third lower risk of dementia than rare or non-consumers, and the highest blueberry consumption has been associated with up to a 50% lower risk.

These studies are observational, so they can't prove that blueberries prevent dementia. But alongside shorter randomized trials showing modest improvements in aspects of memory and cognition with blueberry intake, the long-term signal is intriguing.

I discuss the brain benefits of blueberries and more in the latest episode of the podcast.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick shared the research on blueberries and the ageing brain. Older women in the Nurses' Health Study who ate at least half a cup a week had slower memory decline, about 1.5 to 2.5 years younger in brain terms.

She's upfront that these studies are observational, so they can't prove blueberries prevent dementia. But half a cup a week is cheap and easy.

Frozen ones are fine and usually cheaper. Chuck a handful on your brekky a few times a week. Your brain's worth looking after as much as your back.
hits.video_tip: 15s phone on the bench, tip frozen blueberries onto porridge or yoghurt; captions “Half a cup a week.” then “Frozen is fine. Cheap and easy.”

hits.text:
Your skin ages from the inside out.

Alcohol. Sugar. Dairy. Insulin resistance. Gut imbalances. Falling estrogen. Sun damage.

Dermatologist Dr. Mamina Turegano and I break down what drives skin aging and chronic skin conditions, and what helps.

Full conversation below.
0:00 Strength training, collagen, and healthier skin in midlife;  
3:46 Early exposure to eastern medicine and choosing an MD path 
5:30 Steroids, biologics, and the importance of root-cause medicine 
8:06 Gut health, hormones, and insulin resistance 
10:16 Testing for gut imbalances, SIBO, H. pylori, and hormone patterns 
15:09 Environmental, stress, caffeine, and hormonal factors  
19:07 Functional medicine approaches: gluten, leaky gut, metals, and yeast 
21:15 A healthy skin diet 
22:43 Elimination diets for chronic skin issues: gluten, dairy, sugar, and processed foods 
32:41 Functional medicine success with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis 
41:00 Collagen supplements and lifestyle foundations for skin health 
48:03 Supplements for skin aging: omega-3s, vitamin D, urolithin A, polyphenols 
54:52 Can skin aging be reversed, and the role of strength training

Mark Hyman says your skin ages from the inside out: alcohol, sugar, insulin resistance, gut trouble, and sun damage.

If you work outdoors, that last one's the big one. Years of Aussie sun on your face, neck and arms add up.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Type 2 diabetes starts in your fat cells, but your blood glucose doesn't get meaningfully worse until the problem reaches your muscle.

As fat cells grow too large, they become insulin resistant and pro-inflammatory, both of which promote insulin resistance throughout the body. For a while, the pancreas keeps up by making more insulin, and glucose looks normal. The trouble becomes more pronounced when the insulin resistance reaches your muscle. Muscle is where most of your blood glucose goes when insulin rises, so once muscle stops responding, glucose starts climbing.

Protect your muscle as if your blood glucose depends on it! Ideally, lift two or three times a week (the signal) and prioritize protein and fat (the fuel).
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman says type 2 diabetes starts in your fat cells, but blood sugar only really climbs once the problem reaches your muscle. Muscle is where most of your blood sugar goes.

So your muscle isn't just for lifting gear. It's keeping your blood sugar in check.

His advice: lift two or three times a week for the signal, and put protein and fat on the plate for the fuel. Protect your muscle like your blood sugar depends on it, because it does.
hits.video_tip: 20s face-to-cam, holding a dumbbell or a bag of cement; captions “Muscle soaks up blood sugar.” then “Lift 2–3x a week. Feed it protein.”

hits.draft_en:
Ken Berry's point for anyone on Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro or Zepbound: when you're eating half as much, every bite has to count, or you lose muscle and bone along with the fat.

Eating less only helps if you're still feeding the muscle. Protein first, then everything else. At our age, losing muscle is the one loss you don't want.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
The healthfulness of a food depends on the person who’s eating it.

For example, even higher-carb 'natural' foods can be harmful in people with obesity and insulin resistance, since their bodies may be metabolically ill-equipped to handle that food.

For someone with insulin resistance and obesity, for example, a bowl of oatmeal and fruit can spike blood sugar, increase fat synthesis by the liver, and work against metabolic recovery. 

By contrast, a breakfast of bacon and eggs is far more likely, in the same context, to facilitate metabolic recovery.

This doesn’t make the banana bad. It just reveals that context matters, and sometimes health halos can do more harm than good.

This is from page 10 of my entirely free Beginner’s Guide to Metabolic Health. If this is the kind of information that would help you or a loved one, check below.

No email gate. Nothing. Just my gift to you.

#StayCurious, and spread metabolic health.
hits.draft_en:
Nick Norwitz says how healthy a food is depends on who's eating it. For someone with insulin resistance, a bowl of oats and fruit can spike blood sugar, while bacon and eggs may suit them better.

No food is good or bad for everybody. A health halo doesn't tell you how your body handles it.

If you're carrying weight around the middle, ask your GP to check your fasting insulin and HbA1c. Then you know what breakfast actually suits you.
hits.video_tip: 15–20s phone on the bench, a bowl of oats next to a plate of eggs; captions “Healthy for who?” then “Ask your GP for fasting insulin + HbA1c.”

hits.name: Eric Topol
hits.draft_en:
Eric Topol shared a study on a giant tortoise that has lived 194 years, the oldest land animal alive. Researchers found 287 unique gene variants and less of the random "noise" that usually builds up in DNA with age.

So a fair bit of it is genes, and you can't pick yours.

What you can pick is how you treat what you've got. Keep moving, keep your muscle, sleep properly and get your check-ups. Slow and steady still works.
hits.video_tip: 15s slow walk round the yard or a bush track; captions “194 years. Slow and steady.” then “Can't pick your genes. Can pick your habits.”

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
🚩 Red Flags to Find a New Doctor 🚩

I had an interesting interaction with a clinician this morning that prompted me to write this post. 

It’s not informed by decades of clinical experience; nor by time doing an MD PhD; but by my experiences as a patient.

Let’s start with a joke: What do you call the doctor who graduated at the bottom of their medical school class?

Doctor.

Jokes aside, I don’t mean to doctor bash. To the contrary…

There are some truly remarkable clinicians, including people in my life who I consider bona fide heroes. (see video below 👇 )

And then there is another species of doctor, those who seem to the white coat makes them the arbiter of medical truth. “God complex” is an appropriate term.

In the worst cases, this bleeds into clinical bullying and harmful blanket recommendations blinded by arrogance.

I’ve seen it, and had it aimed at me.

So let me give you three red flags that indicate it’s probably time to find a new doctor.

🚩Red flag #1: They speak in absolutes. 

For example:

“Lower ApoB is always better.”

“Diet and lifestyle can’t change ApoB.”

Medicine is contextual and personalized. When a clinician repeatedly makes broad, definitive statements that are easily falsifiable, even by edge cases, that tells you something.

Maybe they genuinely don’t know better. More likely, and more concerningly, they may believe nuance is unnecessary because the patients and general public couldn’t possibly understand it.

Good clinicians don’t dumb it down to the point of inaccuracy. They teach.

🚩Red flag #2: When challenged fairly, they become defensive rather than curious.

Point out an error and watch what happens.

Do they say, “Interesting. My mistake. Let me look at that and/or learn more”?

Or do they pivot and make the disagreement about you rather than the evidence?

Which brings me to the third red flag.

🚩Red flag #3: They treat questions as insubordination rather than participation.

A good doctor doesn’t need you to obey them. They need you to understand the options well enough to make an informed decision about your own body.

That means explaining means discussing uncertainty and acknowledging trade-offs. 

And it means being willing to say, “I don’t know.”

Bottom line, you have the right to assemble a healthcare team that treats your curiosity as an asset rather than a threat.

The best clinicians I know aren’t threatened by informed patients. They help create them.
hits.draft_en:
Nick Norwitz's red flags that it's time to find a new doctor: they talk in absolutes, they get defensive when you ask a fair question, and they treat questions like insubordination.

A good GP doesn't need you to just do as you're told. They explain your options so you can decide about your own body.

Write your questions down before the appointment and ask every one. If the doctor brushes you off every time, you're allowed to find another one.
hits.video_tip: 20s face-to-cam in the car before an appointment, holding a written list; captions “3 red flags in a doctor.” then “Bring your questions. Ask them.”

Elon Musk's note that Grok @Bot will use whichever back-end model suits the task, Claude Opus 5.5, Midjourney and Suno included, was the biggest post by miles (~67.9M), echoed by Min Choi (~4.4M) and Chubby (~107K). OpenAI's new maths results from an internal frontier model (~18.3M) and Sam Altman's "new era of discovery" (~1.8M) led the science thread, with Demis Hassabis on AI for medicine (~105K), Google Earth AI for disease outbreaks (~118K) and Google's TPUs in orbit (~563K). New drops kept coming: Claude Haiku 5.5 (~2.8M), GPT-6 with Intelligent UI (~2.4M), OpenAI's Decisions API (~1.5M), Cursor agents from your phone (~154K). Trust was the other big thread: Google's SynthID Detector (~657K), ChatGPT watermarks in the EU (~168K), ChatGPT for Teens (~200K), and Claude steering a teenager onto a cliff route that needed a helicopter rescue (~62K). For Tama, the "AI got it wrong, use your own judgment" and "machines can't do your body for you" angles fit a worker voice; the product launches are meta only.
